title: Karatsuba's Algorithm: Overturning a 'Proven' Optimality Conjecture (1960)
explainer: In 1960, Andrey Kolmogorov conjectured in a Moscow State University seminar that the standard grade-school method for multiplying large numbers was asymptotically optimal. Within about a week, his student Anatoly Karatsuba found a faster method using exactly the divide-and-conquer idea this lesson teaches: split each number in half and recombine three smaller multiplications instead of four. It is a clean historical example of a recursive, divide-and-conquer insight overturning what experts believed was settled.

title: The Tower of Hanoi: Origins of a Classic Recursion Puzzle (1883)
explainer: The Tower of Hanoi puzzle was introduced in 1883 by French mathematician Édouard Lucas, published under the pen name "N. Claus de Siam" along with an invented legend about monks moving golden discs. It has been a standard teaching example for recursion ever since, because its cleanest solution is defined entirely in terms of smaller instances of itself: move n-1 discs aside, move the largest disc, then move the n-1 discs back on top.
